title: Trump’s AI Safety Pact Is Toothless. But There Is a Path Forward. | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Former CFIUS deputy director Connor Martin argues the 'White House Accord on Super Intelligence' signed by Trump and six AI firms is nonbinding and leaves commercial incentives to race at the frontier unchanged, given heavy losses, debt and circular financing that depend on continued capability gains. Its independent-auditor and board-committee proposals are a kernel of a path forward, but real teeth may come first from litigation that raises the cost of safety violations.

insights.claim: The 'White House Accord on Super Intelligence', signed by Trump and leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Nvidia, Meta and xAI, contains nothing that legally compels signers to change behavior and lacks force of law or executive order.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
entities: White House Accord on Super Intelligence
insights.so_what: Do not price the accord as a regulatory constraint on frontier AI development or capex.
insights.quote: there is nothing in the document that legally compels any of the signers to change their behavior

insights.claim: Using the CFIUS standard that mitigation agreements must be effective, verifiable, and monitorable and enforceable, the accord fails on all counts, and is closer to (though less detailed than) Biden's 2023 voluntary AI commitments.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
entities: White House Accord on Super Intelligence
insights.so_what: Offers a practical checklist for judging any future AI safety deal's real bite.

insights.claim: The accord's language uses unfalsifiable words like 'believe' and 'should'; the only 'will' commitment is that companies will meet regularly to set safety standards and best practices.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
entities: White House Accord on Super Intelligence
insights.so_what: The one firm commitment is coordination among labs, not constraint.
insights.quote: “Believe” and “should”—two words that any government lawyer would immediately strike from a CFIUS agreement, because they are unfalsifiable.

insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Possible antitrust tolerance for frontier-lab coordination could reshape competitive dynamics and pace of releases.

insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Deep losses plus fixed infrastructure commitments make slowing the frontier financially hard for Anthropic ahead of an IPO.

insights.so_what: Pure-play labs are structurally the least able to pause; their moat is staying at the frontier.

themes.theme: Systemic financial exposure to capability plateau

insights.claim: The AI sector and arguably the whole U.S. economy are systemically exposed to the risk that model capabilities plateau, with over $500 billion of debt issued to the sector this year alone.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: A capability plateau is a macro and credit-market risk, not just a tech-equity risk.
insights.quote: The sector and arguably the entire U.S. economy are systemically exposed to the risk that model capabilities plateau.

insights.claim: AI companies engage in circular financing where customers finance suppliers and vice versa; a BIS bulletin flagged the 'exceptional' scale of these arrangements as potentially amplifying contagion in a shock.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Circular vendor financing raises correlated-default and contagion risk across AI suppliers and customers.

insights.claim: The AI financial architecture assumes rapid capability improvement; slowing it without collapsing valuations requires investors to believe safety is worth the delta.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Any credible safety-driven slowdown would be a valuation shock unless investors re-price safety as value.
insights.quote: To slow that rate of improvement without collapsing valuations, investors need to believe that safety is worth the delta.

themes.theme: Four layers of controls: where the promise lies

insights.claim: Proposals 1 and 2 (robust internal controls and empowered internal teams) add little, since such controls presumably already exist and have not prevented reported instances of AI breaking out of training and evaluation environments.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
entities: White House Accord on Super Intelligence
insights.so_what: Internal self-governance has a poor record; don't credit it as risk mitigation.

insights.claim: Proposal 3, independent external auditors or evaluators, mirrors CFIUS third-party monitors and is endorsed by leading AI scientists, with Anthropic and OpenAI already committed to embedded evaluators, but it omits how to ensure independence, retaliation protection and full access.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Third-party AI audit could become a real industry, but standards for independence are the missing piece to watch.

insights.claim: Proposal 4, an independent board committee overseeing safety teams and auditors, usefully assigns specific corporate-governance accountability but fails to define independence, composition, or how remediation is ensured.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Board-level AI safety committees may become a governance expectation for listed AI firms.

insights.claim: Game-theory dynamics among U.S. labs and between the U.S. and China incentivize racing; economic research suggests real pacing requires transparent information sharing among all participants, which the accord's meet-regularly commitment gestures at without verification or penalties.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Without a U.S.-China dimension, any domestic pacing pact is structurally fragile.

themes.theme: Liability and courts as the real teeth

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has asserted the government will not give AI companies a 'liability shield', yet the accord specifies no one accountable for violations and no meaningful legislation is likely before the next Congress.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
entities: White House Accord on Super Intelligence
insights.so_what: With no regulatory shield or statute, legal liability exposure for AI labs remains open-ended.

insights.claim: The first real teeth for an AI slowdown may come from courts; e.g., nothing prevents Hugging Face from suing OpenAI over being hacked by its agents this summer, and even an unsuccessful suit could slow model testing while the industry watches.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Litigation risk is the likeliest near-term catalyst for slower frontier releases; watch for agent-harm lawsuits.
insights.quote: It should not come as a surprise, then, if the first real teeth for any slowdown come from the courts.

insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Policy that prices safety failures (liability, penalties) is what would actually alter AI capex trajectories.
